summary: Improves how a node connected to several networks chooses among the recursive DNS servers it learns about. Some servers may know private namespaces that others do not, so the document describes ways to pick servers so that names resolve correctly. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If you have several helpers who each know different secrets, you should ask the right one. This memo teaches a computer on many networks which helper to ask for each name.

questions: how to choose dns servers on multi-homed hosts
how does a host choose between dns servers on multiple interfaces
subtitle: How a device on several networks picks which DNS server to ask, using new DHCP options.

tldr.problem: A node connected to several networks may learn several recursive DNS servers, and some of them know private names that the others cannot resolve, so asking the wrong one fails or gives a wrong answer.
tldr.mechanism: New DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options tell the node, for each recursive DNS server, a preference (high, medium or low) and the domains and networks it has special knowledge of; the resolver builds a preference list per query and prefers trusted interfaces.
tldr.outcome: A multi-interfaced node can send private-name queries to the right server and everything else to its default one. The options are not meant to be on by default, because they open a redirection attack vector.

facts.label: Default enablement
facts.value: SHOULD NOT be enabled by default

today: RFC 6731 is a Proposed Standard from December 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Server Choice Matters
sections.content:
A multi-interfaced node (MIF node) is a host or router connected to more than one network at once. Operators sometimes serve private but globally unique namespaces from their Recursive DNS Servers (RDNSSes), so some servers know names that others do not. The node should ask the server that can actually resolve the query.

The RFC gives a web browser as an example: it visits many destinations, each reachable on only one network, so it has to use different interfaces depending on the destination. The document is meant to be combined with tools that deliver routing and address selection policy, such as RFC 4191 and RFC 3442. The wider problem is described in RFC 6418.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are in three different clubs and each club has its own secret nicknames, you need to ask the right club when you want to find someone.

sections.title: The Problems with Private Namespaces
sections.content:
The RFC describes two problems the procedure solves. First, a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) may exist only in a limited scope. A node might have a WLAN link to the public Internet, a cellular link to an operator network and a VPN to an enterprise network. A public name can be resolved by any RDNSS, but an enterprise's private name needs the enterprise's RDNSS, so the node must pick an interface before it even knows the destination's IP address.

Second, the same FQDN may resolve on different interfaces to different addresses that are not globally reachable. The node's routing and address selection must then use the resolved address only with source addresses of the interface where the name was resolved. AAAA record synthesis (RFC 6147) can produce the same effect, since a synthetic record is valid only on the network that synthesized it. Even a single-homed node can be hurt if it keeps a DNS cache after moving to a new network.

The solution is only partial for names that mean different peers, or different services, on different interfaces. Those higher-layer issues may be solvable only by manual user intervention, although DNSSEC validation can help in some cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the same name points to a different house depending on which street you ask on, and sometimes a name only exists on one street.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Three scenarios shaped the design. In each, the private network's server is given low preference and a list of the domains it knows, while the default server keeps medium preference.

  • CPE: a home gateway with two uplinks, one to the Internet and one to a private network. Default queries go to the Internet uplink's server, and private-namespace queries go to the private network's server.
  • Cellular: a device with WLAN and cellular up. WLAN is used by default, which likely saves power and often gives lower latency, while the operator's private names go through the cellular interface. Cellular is typically considered trusted and WLAN often untrusted.
  • VPN: local access network by default, and the enterprise's server over the VPN for enterprise names. The VPN is considered trusted and the local network untrusted.

In dual-stack networks, either or both of DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 can deliver the information.
sections.plainLanguage: At home, on a phone or on a work VPN, the rule is the same: ask the usual helper for ordinary names, and ask the special helper only for the special names.

sections.title: Choosing and Prioritizing Servers
sections.content:
The resolver SHALL build a preference list of RDNSSes for each query, after requesting selection information with the DHCP options before any DNS query. Servers learned by other means (DHCPv6 OPTION_DNS_SERVERS from RFC 3646, the DHCPv4 Domain Server option from RFC 2132, or the Router Advertisement RDNSS option from RFC 6106) count as default servers with medium preference.

For a query, the resolver MUST give the highest preference to servers known to serve a matching domain or network, MUST prefer servers of trusted interfaces, and MUST NOT rank a less trusted server above a trusted one even if it seems to have more information. Between equally trusted servers it uses the option's preference field.

Requests go out in list order until an acceptable reply arrives, all replies arrive, or a timeout occurs. If the name matches a specific domain or network rule, a DNSSEC-aware resolver MUST NOT accept an unvalidated reply until all servers on the list have been contacted or timed out, which protects against redirection. A validated NXDOMAIN from a server that can answer the name means non-validated replies from others MUST NOT be accepted.

Follow-up queries (for example after a CNAME or DNAME) MUST use the same interface. If DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 conflict on equally trusted interfaces, DHCPv6 MUST be preferred unless DHCPv4 has extra security protection. Cached private-namespace data should not outlive the interface it came from, so implementations SHOULD keep per-interface caches or flush on interface change.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer makes a ranked list of helpers for each question. It asks the trusted helper who knows that topic first, and it double-checks answers when the topic is a special one.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 and DHCPv4 Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option is OPTION_RDNSS_SELECTION (74). It carries the RDNSS IPv6 address, a 2-bit preference field prf, and a variable-length list of domains and networks encoded as in Section 8 of RFC 3315. The DHCPv4 option is RDNSS Selection (146), with primary and secondary RDNSS IPv4 addresses (the secondary is 0.0.0.0 if not configured) and the same domains and networks list.

Preference values are 01 High, 00 Medium and 11 Low. 10 is Reserved: it MUST NOT be sent and MUST be treated as Medium on receipt. The special domain . marks a server that can resolve global names and act as a default; without it the server only knows the listed domains and networks. Reverse-lookup networks use the IP6.ARPA (RFC 3596) or IN-ADDR.ARPA (RFC 2317) forms.

The list of networks MUST cover all the configured domains and SHOULD use long prefixes to avoid collisions. A DHCPv6 client SHOULD include the Option Request Option listing the option code to signal support. If DHCPv4 data exceeds 255 octets, multiple options MAY be used as in RFC 3396. New information for a server already known is appended, previously obtained information MUST NOT be removed, and a conflicting server address from a less trusted interface MUST be ignored. Clients SHALL refresh the information on link-state changes and when renewing address lifetimes or leases.
sections.plainLanguage: The network hands the computer a card for each helper: who they are, how important they are, and which topics they know.

sections.title: Limits and Advice for Administrators
sections.content:
The options are size-limited by DHCP messages, so they suit deployments where relatively few, carefully chosen domains and networks are enough. They SHOULD NOT be enabled by default. They are acceptable when the option arrives over a secure trusted channel, when the client does DNSSEC validation, when the resolver validates and is reached over a trusted channel, or when the recommended server is already known and trusted by the client. Because DHCP cannot tell which of these holds, the option needs explicit enabling by administrative means or by a client that knows it validates.

Administrators must keep private namespaces globally unique, with exceptions such as .local, and they MUST be subdomains of domains for which the operator provides authoritative service. Deploying DNSSEC for the zone is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The special cards are switched off until someone says it is safe to use them, because a fake card could send you to the wrong helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attackers might use these options to redirect some or all of a resolver's queries, for denial of service or as preparation for a man-in-the-middle attack. They might advertise domains and networks of very small to very large scope, or try to make their own server the highest-preference default.

The best countermeasure is a validating, DNSSEC-aware resolver. Trusting an RDNSS's validation is possible only if the node trusts that server and uses a secure channel. Trust levels of interfaces are implementation and deployment dependent. An authenticated, encrypted VPN or a connection to a trusted home or cellular network might be trusted, while an unauthenticated connection to an unknown visited network would likely be untrusted. The RFC uses normative language for the algorithm so nodes do not open new attack vectors by accident.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could hand you a fake card to make you ask the wrong helper, so the computer double-checks answers and trusts some networks more than others.

sections.title: A Worked Example and Alternatives
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a node open interface 1 and learn domain1.example.com and an IPv6 reverse network from its DHCPv6 server, then open interface 2 and learn domain2.example.com and its network. When an application asks for private.domain2.example.com, the node ranks the servers, picks interface 2 and resolves the name there.

Appendix A lists practices for networks without this support: querying on several interfaces in parallel (which costs power and server load), using DNS search list options as hints, using more-specific routes, or the longest matching prefix for reverse lookups. Appendix B notes that a validator with multiple trust anchors can use which anchor validated an answer as evidence of which interface to rely on. Appendix C gives non-normative C-style pseudocode for the selection logic.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer remembers which topics each helper knows. When you ask about a topic, it goes straight to the helper who knows it.
